sourceBindings.text: A texture result helps you ask better questions about a crop. Combine it with drainage, water, nutrients and local growing conditions before making a recommendation.
Compare sandy, clay-rich and loamy soil without confusing nutrient retention with measured nutrient supply.
Propose at least two justified crop candidates for each tested sample and explain the conditions that still need checking.
Explain the heavy-soil carrot case and evaluate a suitable alternative without assuming all clay is waterlogged.

sourceBindings.text: A grower wants carrots in a compacted bed that stays wet.
Separate the clay-rich texture from observed compaction and persistent wetness.
Explain possible root-growth and root-health problems.
Discuss cabbage or broccoli only after adequate drainage and aeration are established; otherwise investigate the site first.
An alternative crop is not a substitute for solving a drainage problem.

sourceBindings.text: One learner chooses corn for a sandy sample and another for loam.
Both may be reasonable candidates under suitable conditions.
The sandy site may need more careful water and nutrient-retention management.
Check each justification and site information instead of marking one wrong solely because the same name appears in two lists.
Assess the reason and conditions, not a unique crop-to-soil pairing.

sourceBindings.text: For each of three tested sandy, clay-rich and loamy samples, choose two possible crops and explain the conditions that would make each reasonable. Then reconsider carrots in a compacted wet bed.
Use measured texture and observed drainage, not colour alone, to support each candidate.
State what water, nutrients, pH, salinity, season and local crop information is still missing.
Explain why a loose rooting zone helps the carrot example and why wet, compacted clay is a management issue rather than a universal ban on a crop.
Compare two learners who choose the same crop for different soils and judge their reasoning rather than insisting on one pairing.
Use the earlier observed texture evidence; this guided comparison does not certify a new field skill.
